# Overview

`sdmhelpers` provides helper functions for species distribution modelling (SDM)
workflows, with particular emphasis on presence-background models implemented
with `maxnet`. The package contains tools for constructing sampling-bias
surfaces from target-group records, weighting target-group observations by
seasonal or combined seasonal and diel overlap, selecting complete spatial
folds for independent testing, screening environmental predictors, and
evaluating predictions using the True Skill Statistic (TSS).

Presence-only SDMs are sensitive to differences between the sampling process
that generated species observations and the process used to select background
locations. A commonly used approach is therefore to select or weight background
data so that they reflect similar sampling bias to the presence data
[@phillips2009; @elith2011]. `sdmhelpers` extends this idea by allowing records
from a target group to contribute unequally according to their temporal
similarity to the focal species.

The examples below use datasets distributed with `sdmhelpers`. They are reduced
or pseudonymised datasets intended for demonstrating package functionality, not
for biological inference.

`sdmhelpers` was developed as part of the project *HiQBioDiv:
High-resolution quantification of biodiversity for conservation and
management*, funded by the Latvian Council of Science
(Ref. No. VPP-VARAM-DABA-2024/1-0002).

The development version can be installed from GitHub with:

```{r install, eval = FALSE}
# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("aavotins/sdmhelpers")
```

Packages used in this vignette:


```{r setup}
library(sdmhelpers)
library(sf)
library(ggplot2)
library(terra)
library(maxnet)
library(SDMtune)
library(ENMeval)
```



# Example data

Several example datasets are included in the package. The examples in this
vignette use bird and bryophyte observations, spatial presence and background
locations, spatial blocks, a 100-m grid, known habitat-inventory dates, and an
example environmental raster.

```{r data}
data("aves_small", package = "sdmhelpers")
data("bryophyta_one", package = "sdmhelpers")
data("habitat_inventories", package = "sdmhelpers")
data("points100", package = "sdmhelpers")
data("example_grid", package = "sdmhelpers")
example_grid <- terra::unwrap(example_grid)
data("example_presences", package = "sdmhelpers")
data("example_background", package = "sdmhelpers")
data("example_independent_blocks", package = "sdmhelpers")
data("egv_names", package = "sdmhelpers")
```

The environmental raster used later in the vignette is stored in
`inst/extdata`.

```{r env-path}
egv_file <- system.file("extdata",
                        "example_egv.tif",
                        package = "sdmhelpers")

```

# Simple target-group bias surface

Target-group background sampling uses observations of taxa that are expected to
have been collected through a sampling process similar to that of the focal
species. If sampling effort is spatially biased, drawing background data from
the same biased sampling domain can reduce the contrast between presence and
background sampling processes [@phillips2009].

Here, one species from `aves_small` is treated as the focal species while all 
species form the target group. For this example, the focal species is chosen
programmatically as the species with the largest number of records so that the
example does not depend on a particular species name.

```{r simple-target-group}
target_species <- names(
  sort(table(aves_small$species), decreasing = TRUE)
)[1]

target_species

target_group <- aves_small
```

Multiple observations can occur in the same 100-m grid cell. For the spatial
bias surface, records are therefore counted by grid cell and supplied to
`kde_surface()` as weights.

```{r simple-target-group-points}
tg_counts <- aggregate(
  list(n_records = rep(1, nrow(target_group))),
  by = list(id100 = target_group$id100),
  FUN = sum
)

idx <- match(tg_counts$id100, points100$id)
keep <- !is.na(idx)

tg_points <- points100[idx[keep], ]
tg_points$n_records <- tg_counts$n_records[keep]

tg_points

```

`kde_surface()` first bins point weights to the reference raster and then
applies Gaussian smoothing. This makes the calculation practical for large
rasters and large bandwidths. Kernel density estimation in general is described
by @silverman1986.

The example grid uses EPSG:3059, whose map units are metres, so `sigma = 3000`
corresponds to a Gaussian bandwidth of 3 km. With `normalize = "pdf"`, the
resulting surface is normalised to integrate to one and represents a 
probability-density-scaled surface of the spatial distribution of target-group 
records. It can therefore be used as a relative proxy sampling-bias surface for 
background sampling.


```{r simple-kde, eval=TRUE, fig.cap = "Unweighted target-group sampling-bias surface."}
simple_bias <- kde_surface(
  x = tg_points,
  weight_field = "n_records",
  sigma = 3000,
  ref = example_grid,
  normalize = "pdf",
  mask = TRUE
)

options(scipen = 999)
terra::plot(simple_bias, main = "Simple target-group bias")
```

This simple approach assumes that every target-group record is equally
informative about the sampling process affecting the focal species. The following 
sections relax that assumption.


# Phenologically weighted target-group

Species observed by the same people or recording scheme may nevertheless have
different seasonal detectability, availability, or both. A species recorded mainly in winter, for 
example, may provide little information about sampling effort relevant to a
species recorded mainly during late spring.


phenology_overlap_weights() estimates overlap between species' day-of-year 
distributions using overlapping::overlap() [@pastore2019]. This approach 
provides compatibility with conventional kernel-density overlap estimation [@pastore2018]. 
However, because day of year is treated as a linear variable, observations 
near the end and beginning of the calendar year are not considered adjacent. 
For species with observation periods spanning this boundary, 
torus_overlap_many() provides an alternative based on circular 
kernel-density estimation with constant (e.g. midday) value for the time of day. 

First, day of year is added to the bird records.

```{r phenology-data}
bird_dates <- aves_small
bird_dates$DoY <- as.POSIXlt(bird_dates$date)$yday + 1L

target_code <- bird_dates$code[
  match(target_species, bird_dates$species)
]

target_code
```

We then estimate phenological overlap between the focal species (synonymous to 
target-species) and every species in the target-group.

```{r phenology-overlap}
phenology_weights <- phenology_overlap_weights(
  target = bird_dates,
  group = bird_dates,
  target_code = target_code,
  target_id = "code",
  group_id = "code",
  target_doy = "DoY",
  group_doy = "DoY",
  type = "2",
  min_n = 5
)

phenology_weights[
  order(phenology_weights$weight, decreasing = TRUE),
]
```

The returned `weight` values sum to one across comparison species with valid
overlap estimates. Here, each target-group observation receives the weight of
its species. Records are then summed within 100-m cells before KDE smoothing.

```{r phenology-weighted-points}
target_group_p <- merge(
  target_group,
  phenology_weights[, c("code", "weight")],
  by = "code",
  all.x = TRUE
)

target_group_p <- target_group_p[
  is.finite(target_group_p$weight) &
    !is.na(target_group_p$id100),
]

tg_weighted <- aggregate(
  list(weight = target_group_p$weight),
  by = list(id100 = target_group_p$id100),
  FUN = sum
)

idx <- match(tg_weighted$id100, points100$id)
keep <- !is.na(idx)

tg_points_weighted <- points100[idx[keep], ]
tg_points_weighted$weight <- tg_weighted$weight[keep]
```

```{r phenology-kde, fig.cap = "Phenologically weighted target-group sampling-bias surface."}
phenology_bias <- kde_surface(
  x = tg_points_weighted,
  weight_field = "weight",
  sigma = 3000,
  ref = example_grid,
  normalize = "pdf",
  mask = TRUE
)

options(scipen = 999)
terra::plot(
  phenology_bias,
  main = "Phenologically weighted target-group bias"
)
```

The weighted surface should be interpreted as a relative sampling-bias surface,
not as an estimate of species occurrence probability. Its purpose is to
describe where observations relevant to the focal species' seasonal sampling
process were more or less likely to have been collected.

# Target-group weighting by seasonal and diel overlap

For taxa whose detectability varies both seasonally and through the day,
seasonal overlap alone may be insufficient. `torus_overlap_many()` represents
season and time of day as two circular dimensions and estimates overlap on a
two-dimensional torus. Circular treatment is important because both annual and
daily cycles wrap around their endpoints; see @mardia2000 for directional
statistics and @ridout2009 for overlap estimation of diel activity patterns.

The bird dataset contains date-time observations. For this introductory example, 
we select the focal species with the largest number of valid date-time 
records and compare its seasonal and diel observation distributions with 
those of every species in the target group (including the focal species itself).

```{r torus-data}
comparison_data <- aves_small[
  !is.na(aves_small$date_time),
  ,
  drop = FALSE
]

target_species_torus <- names(
  sort(table(comparison_data$species), decreasing = TRUE)
)[1]

reference_data <- comparison_data[
  comparison_data$species == target_species_torus,
  ,
  drop = FALSE
]

reference_data$obs_date <- as.Date(reference_data$date_time)
reference_data$obs_time <- hms::as_hms(reference_data$date_time)

comparison_data$obs_date <- as.Date(comparison_data$date_time)
comparison_data$obs_time <- hms::as_hms(comparison_data$date_time)


```

For speed, the example uses a coarser evaluation grid than would often be used
in a final analysis.

```{r torus-overlap}
torus_result <- torus_overlap_many(
  reference_data = reference_data,
  comparison_data = comparison_data,
  comparison_group_col = "species",
  reference_date_col = "obs_date",
  reference_time_col = "obs_time",
  comparison_date_col = "obs_date",
  comparison_time_col = "obs_time",
  reference_name = target_species_torus,
  season_bw_days = 14,
  daily_bw_hours = 1,
  date_resolution_days = 7,
  time_resolution_minutes = 60,
  min_n = 5,
  return_density = FALSE
)

torus_overlap <- torus_result$overlap
torus_overlap <- torus_overlap[
  order(torus_overlap$overlap, decreasing = TRUE),
]

head(torus_overlap, 10)
```

The overlap coefficient ranges from zero to one for normalised densities. A
large value indicates that a comparison species has a seasonal-diel observation
distribution similar to the focal species.

To use these coefficients as relative species weights in a target group, they
can be normalised across comparison species.

```{r torus-weights}
ok <- is.finite(torus_overlap$overlap)

torus_overlap$weight <- NA_real_
torus_overlap$weight[ok] <-
  torus_overlap$overlap[ok] /
  sum(torus_overlap$overlap[ok])

head(
  torus_overlap[
    order(torus_overlap$weight, decreasing = TRUE),
    c("comparison", "overlap", "weight")
  ],
  10
)
```

These weights can be joined back to the individual observations and passed to
`kde_surface()` in exactly the same way as the phenological weights above.

The overlap can also be visualised, when setting `return_density = TRUE`

```{r torus-plot}
torus_result <- torus_overlap_many(
  reference_data = reference_data,
  comparison_data = comparison_data,
  comparison_group_col = "species",
  reference_date_col = "obs_date",
  reference_time_col = "obs_time",
  comparison_date_col = "obs_date",
  comparison_time_col = "obs_time",
  reference_name = target_species_torus,
  season_bw_days = 14,
  daily_bw_hours = 1,
  date_resolution_days = 7,
  time_resolution_minutes = 60,
  min_n = 5,
  return_density = TRUE
)

ggplot(torus_result$density,
       aes(
         x = seasonal_position_days,
         y = decimal_hour,
         fill = comparison_density
         )
       ) +
  geom_raster() +
  facet_wrap(~ comparison) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 24, by = 3)) +
  viridis::scale_fill_viridis() +
  labs(
    x = "Seasonal position (days from 1 January)",
       y = "Time of day",
       fill = "Density",
       title = "Species-specific registration activity") +
  theme_bw()

ggplot(torus_result$density,
       aes(
         x = seasonal_position_days,
         y = decimal_hour,
         fill = shared_density
         )
       ) +
  geom_raster() +
  facet_wrap(~ comparison) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 24, by = 3)) +
  viridis::scale_fill_viridis() +
  labs(x = "Seasonal position (days from 1 January)",
       y = "Time of day",
       fill = "Density",
       title = paste0(
         "Registration activity overlap with ", 
         target_species_torus
         )
       ) +
  theme_bw()


```


# Known inventory dates

Sometimes the dates of a survey or habitat inventory are known, while the
species itself was not necessarily recorded during that survey. In this case,
`doy_kde_weights()` can estimate how closely each inventory date corresponds to
the seasonal registration-activity distribution of a target species.

The function estimates a circular approximation to a day-of-year KDE from the 
reference dates and evaluates that density at another set of dates. Circularity 
is approximated by periodically extending the reference observations across the 
seasonal boundary, which reduces boundary effects between observations near the 
end and beginning of the year. Bandwidth controls the degree of smoothing, 
as in conventional KDE
[@silverman1986].

The example below uses one bryophyte species considered to be an old-growth 
forest specialist and therefore specifically searched for during habitat inventories.

```{r known-dates}
bryophyta_species <- names(
  sort(table(bryophyta_one$species), decreasing = TRUE)
)[1]

reference_dates <- bryophyta_one$date[
  bryophyta_one$species == bryophyta_species &
    !is.na(bryophyta_one$date)
]

inventory_keep <- !is.na(habitat_inventories$date)

inventory_weights <- doy_kde_weights(
  A_dates = reference_dates,
  B_dates = habitat_inventories$date[inventory_keep],
  scale = "percentile_A",
  bw = "nrd0"
)

weighted_inventories <- habitat_inventories[inventory_keep, ]
weighted_inventories$phenology_weight <- inventory_weights$weights
```

With `scale = "percentile_A"`, weights describe how high the estimated
reference density is relative to density values across the seasonal cycle.
They are relative phenological correspondence scores rather than occurrence
probabilities.

```{r inventory-summary}
aggregate(
  phenology_weight ~ habitat_type,
  data = weighted_inventories,
  FUN = mean
)
```

The estimated seasonal reference curve can also be inspected directly.

```{r inventory-density, fig.cap = "Estimated seasonal registration-activity curve used for weighting known inventory dates."}
plot(
  inventory_weights$density$x,
  inventory_weights$density$y,
  type = "l",
  xlab = "Day of year",
  ylab = "Estimated reference density"
)
```



# Selecting an independent testing set

Random train-test splitting can give overly optimistic estimates of predictive
performance when nearby observations are spatially dependent. Spatially
structured resampling is therefore generally preferable when the intended
prediction involves geographic transfer [@roberts2017].

`sdmhelpers` does not define the spatial blocks themselves. Instead,
`select_folds_by_quota()` and `select_joint_folds()` select complete groups from
fold identifiers created elsewhere. Independence therefore comes from the
design of the folds, not from the selection function.

The package contains example presence records, background records, and
independent spatial polygons.

```{r spatial-folds}
pres_sf <- sf::st_as_sf(
  example_presences,
  coords = c("x", "y"),
  crs = 3059
)

bg_sf <- sf::st_as_sf(
  example_background,
  coords = c("x", "y"),
  crs = 3059
)

block_id <- setdiff(
  names(example_independent_blocks),
  attr(example_independent_blocks, "sf_column")
)[1]

pres_joined <- sf::st_join(
  pres_sf,
  example_independent_blocks[block_id],
  join = sf::st_within,
  left = TRUE
)

bg_joined <- sf::st_join(
  bg_sf,
  example_independent_blocks[block_id],
  join = sf::st_within,
  left = TRUE
)

pres_folds <- pres_joined[[block_id]]
bg_folds <- bg_joined[[block_id]]
```

When both presences and background should be withheld from the same spatial
blocks, `select_joint_folds()` is convenient.

```{r joint-fold-selection}
independent <- select_joint_folds(
  pres_folds = pres_folds,
  bg_folds = bg_folds,
  target_prop = 0.25,
  pres_bounds = c(0.20, 0.30),
  bg_bounds = c(0.20, 0.30),
  max_tries = 3000,
  bg_match_weight = 1,
  seed = 1,
  print_report = FALSE
)

independent$selected_fold_ids
independent$summary[c(
  "n_pres_selected",
  "n_bg_selected",
  "prop_pres_selected",
  "prop_bg_selected"
)]
```

The returned logical vectors preserve the row order of the input data and can
be used directly for subsetting.

```{r split-independent}
pres_test <- example_presences[independent$pres_selected_idx, ]
pres_train <- example_presences[!independent$pres_selected_idx, ]

bg_test <- example_background[independent$bg_selected_idx, ]
bg_train <- example_background[!independent$bg_selected_idx, ]

c(
  pres_train = nrow(pres_train),
  pres_test = nrow(pres_test),
  bg_train = nrow(bg_train),
  bg_test = nrow(bg_test)
)
```

If only one type of observation needs to be selected, the simpler
`select_folds_by_quota()` can be used instead.

```{r one-set-fold-selection}
presence_only_selection <- select_folds_by_quota(
  folds = pres_folds,
  target_prop = 0.25,
  bounds = c(0.20, 0.30),
  seed = 1,
  print_report = FALSE
)

presence_only_selection$summary$prop_selected
```


# Screening predictor variance

Predictors that are constant across all data used for model fitting cannot
provide an estimable environmental response. Low variance within an individual
subset, however, does not necessarily imply that a predictor is uninformative:
for example, a predictor may be constant among presences but variable among
background records. `screen_egv_variance()` therefore distinguishes the
presence, background, and combined-data checks and records which checks
contribute to predictor selection.

The example environmental raster contains five ecogeographical variables.
The presence and background locations were split spatially into independent
training and testing sets in the preceding section.

```{r egv}
env <- terra::rast(egv_file)
env
```

We first prepare the training and independent-testing datasets **once**, using
the same environmental predictors. `SDMtune::prepareSWD()` removes locations
with missing values in any supplied environmental layer. Many example records
fall outside the raster's complete-data domain; the counts below show how many
observations remain after extraction. All subsequent checks, fold assignments,
model fitting, and evaluation use these retained records.

```{r prepare-swd}
training_set <- SDMtune::prepareSWD(
  species = "example_species",
  p = pres_train,
  a = bg_train,
  env = env,
  verbose = FALSE
)

testing_set <- SDMtune::prepareSWD(
  species = "example_species",
  p = pres_test,
  a = bg_test,
  env = env,
  verbose = FALSE
)

c(
  training_presences = sum(training_set@pa == 1),
  training_background = sum(training_set@pa == 0),
  testing_presences = sum(testing_set@pa == 1),
  testing_background = sum(testing_set@pa == 0)
)
```

For spatial cross-validation, we assign folds **after** the environmental-value
extraction so that the fold identifiers correspond exactly to rows in the
training `SWD` object. `ENMeval::get.block()` expects longitude-latitude
coordinates; the projected EPSG:3059 coordinates are therefore converted to
EPSG:4326 solely for constructing the folds. This does not change the predictor
values stored in `training_set`.

```{r training-cv-folds}
as_lonlat <- function(coords) {
  pts <- sf::st_as_sf(
    coords,
    coords = c("X", "Y"),
    crs = 3059
  )
  ll <- sf::st_coordinates(sf::st_transform(pts, 4326))
  data.frame(lon = ll[, 1], lat = ll[, 2])
}

pres_idx <- training_set@pa == 1
bg_idx <- training_set@pa == 0

block_folds <- ENMeval::get.block(
  occs = as_lonlat(training_set@coords[pres_idx, , drop = FALSE]),
  bg = as_lonlat(training_set@coords[bg_idx, , drop = FALSE])
)
```

The screen checks presences, backgrounds, and their combination both across
all training records and within each cross-validation training partition.
Because `bg_folds` is supplied, the corresponding held-out background fold is
excluded as well as the presence fold. Presence-only checks are retained as
diagnostics but do not automatically remove predictors. The independent test
set can also be diagnosed, while the default leakage-safe settings ensure that
its values do not affect `keep` or `remove`.

```{r variance-screen}
variance_screen <- screen_egv_variance(
  train = training_set,
  test = testing_set,
  occ_folds = block_folds$occs.grp,
  bg_folds = block_folds$bg.grp,
  env = env,
  env_sample_n = 5000L,
  seed = 1L,
  sd_tol = 0,
  check_presences = TRUE,
  check_background = TRUE,
  check_combined = TRUE,
  presence_affects_selection = FALSE,
  include_test_bg = FALSE,
  check_test = TRUE,
  test_affects_selection = FALSE,
  verbose = FALSE
)

variance_screen$keep
variance_screen$remove
```

A predictor is removed only if it fails at least one check marked
`used_for_selection = TRUE`. A failed diagnostic-only check remains visible in
`diagnostics` but does not affect predictor selection. Even though this example
calculates diagnostic-only checks on the independent test, their results must
not be used to revise the chosen predictor set or model. In a final analysis,
it is preferable not to inspect the held-out test diagnostics until the model
specification has been fixed.

```{r variance-diagnostics}
head(variance_screen$diagnostics)

subset(
  variance_screen$diagnostics,
  failed & !used_for_selection,
  select = c(check, subset, group, variable, sd, reason)
)

```

The random environmental-domain check samples raster cells independently of
the observed training background locations. It does **not** resample the
background records already contained in `training_set`.

A common predictor set screened across all CV partitions is convenient for
this introductory example. For an unbiased assessment of a pipeline that
selects predictors anew, that selection must instead be performed separately
inside each CV training partition.

```{r}
subset(
  variance_screen$diagnostics,
  check == "cv_training",
  select = c(
    check, subset, group, fold,
    variable, sd, failed, used_for_selection
  )
)

```





# Fitting a small maxnet model

`sdmhelpers` supports rather than replaces SDM software. Here we fit a small
illustrative `maxnet` model to the training data using **only the predictors
retained by the variance screen**. This model is for demonstration; the
cross-validation example below can be used to compare alternative feature
classes and regularisation multipliers before fitting a final model.

```{r fit-maxnet}
selected_vars <- variance_screen$keep

if (!length(selected_vars)) {
  stop("No predictors passed variance screening.")
}

maxnet_model <- maxnet::maxnet(
  p = training_set@pa,
  data = training_set@data[, selected_vars, drop = FALSE],
  addsamplestobackground = TRUE
)
```

Following the conventional Maxent approach, presence locations not already
represented in the background are additionally included as background samples
during model fitting. This behaviour is enabled by
`addsamplestobackground = TRUE`, which is also the default in `maxnet`.

We do not separately call `SDMtune::addSamplesToBg()` because `maxnet`
handles this operation internally. Consequently, the original `training_set`
object remains unchanged, and its presence and background records can be
used consistently for subsequent evaluation and cross-validation.

Importantly, this operation uses only the training data. Independent testing
presences and background records remain withheld from model fitting.

# Evaluating models with TSS

The true skill statistic (TSS) is defined as

\[
\mathrm{TSS} = \mathrm{sensitivity} + \mathrm{specificity} - 1.
\]

`max_tss()` evaluates candidate thresholds and returns the threshold that
maximizes TSS, together with sensitivity and specificity. For
presence-background data, background locations are not confirmed absences;
thus the reported specificity is the proportion of background records
classified as negative, and TSS should be interpreted as
presence-background discrimination rather than classification accuracy
against known absences [@allouche2006].

Critically, selecting a threshold using independent-test predictions and then
reporting TSS on that same test set would yield a test-optimized estimate. Here
we select the threshold using **training predictions only**, and then apply
it unchanged to the withheld independent test. The resulting independent-test
TSS is not optimized on test labels, although the threshold chosen on fitting
data may be optimistic for the training sample itself.

```{r training-threshold}
train_p_pos <- predict(
  maxnet_model,
  newdata = training_set@data[
    training_set@pa == 1, selected_vars, drop = FALSE
  ],
  type = "cloglog"
)

train_p_bg <- predict(
  maxnet_model,
  newdata = training_set@data[
    training_set@pa == 0, selected_vars, drop = FALSE
  ],
  type = "cloglog"
)

training_tss <- max_tss(p_pos = train_p_pos, p_neg = train_p_bg)
threshold <- unname(training_tss["threshold"])
training_tss
```

```{r independent-predictions}
test_p_pos <- predict(
  maxnet_model,
  newdata = testing_set@data[
    testing_set@pa == 1, selected_vars, drop = FALSE
  ],
  type = "cloglog"
)

test_p_bg <- predict(
  maxnet_model,
  newdata = testing_set@data[
    testing_set@pa == 0, selected_vars, drop = FALSE
  ],
  type = "cloglog"
)

independent_sensitivity <- mean(test_p_pos >= threshold)
independent_background_specificity <- mean(test_p_bg < threshold)

c(
  threshold_from_training = threshold,
  sensitivity = independent_sensitivity,
  background_specificity = independent_background_specificity,
  independent_TSS = independent_sensitivity +
    independent_background_specificity - 1
)
```

The same threshold can be applied to predictions at raster cells when a binary
suitability map is needed. For an independent final evaluation, the threshold
and all predictor-selection and tuning decisions should be fixed before the
held-out test predictions are examined.

# Cross-validation TSS with ENMeval

The independent testing set created earlier is reserved for the final assessment 
of the fitted model. Model tuning instead uses spatial cross-validation of the 
training data, keeping the independent testing set out of predictor-selection 
and tuning decisions. Spatial resampling can reduce dependence between model 
calibration and validation observations when the intended prediction involves 
geographic transfer [@roberts2017].

`ENMeval` supports spatial partitions and multiple complexity settings for Maxent 
and `maxnet` models [@muscarella2014; @kass2021]. We reuse the four presence and 
background fold assignments (`block_folds`) created in the predictor-screening 
section. These were calculated using the records remaining in `training_set` 
after environmental values were extracted, so their ordering matches the model 
inputs. There is no need to generate a second set of folds.

For illustration, we compare three feature-class settings (linear, `L`; 
quadratic, `Q`; and linear plus quadratic, `LQ`) and three regularisation 
multipliers (0.5, 1, and 2). The regularisation multiplier controls the strength 
of model penalisation; thus, nine candidate settings are evaluated.

**Important:** The predictor set used below is the one returned 
by `screen_egv_variance()` in the preceding section. It is held constant across 
the candidate model settings for this introductory example.

```{r enmeval-inputs}
selected_vars <- variance_screen$keep

if (length(selected_vars) == 0L) {
  stop("No predictors passed variance screening.")
}

pres_idx <- training_set@pa == 1
bg_idx <- training_set@pa == 0

# The as_lonlat() helper and block_folds were defined in the preceding section.
# ENMeval receives coordinates in the first two columns, followed by predictors.
presences <- cbind(
  as_lonlat(training_set@coords[pres_idx, , drop = FALSE]),
  training_set@data[pres_idx, selected_vars, drop = FALSE]
)

background <- cbind(
  as_lonlat(training_set@coords[bg_idx, , drop = FALSE]),
  training_set@data[bg_idx, selected_vars, drop = FALSE]
)

stopifnot(
  length(block_folds$occs.grp) == nrow(presences),
  length(block_folds$bg.grp) == nrow(background)
)
```

Following the conventional Maxent approach, occurrence locations are additionally 
included among the background samples used for model fitting by setting 
`addsamplestobackground = TRUE`. This behavior is the default in both `maxnet` 
and ENMeval's Maxnet implementation. During spatial cross-validation, only the 
training data for each partition should contribute to model fitting, while 
validation presences and backgrounds remain withheld for evaluation. The 
option `validation.bg = "partition"` additionally restricts validation comparisons 
to the background records assigned to the corresponding validation partition.

```{r enmeval-tuning, message=FALSE}
enmeval_result <- ENMeval::ENMevaluate(
  occs = presences,
  bg = background,
  algorithm = "maxnet",
  partitions = "user",
  user.grp = list(
    occs.grp = block_folds$occs.grp,
    bg.grp = block_folds$bg.grp
  ),
  tune.args = list(
    fc = c("L", "Q", "LQ"),
    rm = c(0.5, 1, 2)
  ),
  other.settings = list(
    validation.bg = "partition",
    addsamplestobackground = TRUE
  ),
  user.eval = tss_user_eval
)
```

The `user.eval = tss_user_eval` argument adds the package's custom TSS calculations. 
For each candidate model and cross-validation fold, `ENMeval` supplies predictions 
for training and validation occurrences and background records. `tss_user_eval()` 
applies `max_tss()` separately to the training and validation predictions. Its 
fold-level output includes maximum validation TSS (`tss.val`), the corresponding 
validation threshold (`thr.val`), sensitivity (`sens.val`), background-based 
specificity (`spec.val`), and maximum training TSS (`tss.train`).

In presence-background models, background locations are not confirmed absences. 
Consequently, `spec.val` is the proportion of background predictions below the 
selected threshold, not specificity estimated using verified absences.

**Interpretation of threshold optimisation.** Since `thr.val` is selected to 
maximise TSS on the same validation observations used to calculate `tss.val`, 
validation TSS is optimised for that fold. The spatial validation records were 
withheld from *model fitting*, but not from *threshold selection*. Accordingly, 
these TSS values can help compare candidate settings, but should not be presented 
as fully independent estimates of the performance of a preselected classification 
threshold. For a final independent threshold-based assessment, select the threshold 
without reference to the independent test outcomes and apply it unchanged to that 
test set, as described in the preceding evaluation section.

The model-level results aggregate values across folds. A compact table is more 
useful in an introductory vignette than printing every available statistic:

```{r enmeval-results}
cv_results <- ENMeval::eval.results(enmeval_result)

knitr::kable(
  cv_results[, c(
    "fc", "rm", "auc.val.avg",
    "tss.val.avg", "tss.val.sd",
    "AICc", "delta.AICc"
  )],
  digits = 3
)
```

Here, the Continuous Boyce Index (`CBI`) is available only when the 
optional `ecospat` dependency is installed. Moreover, because the example passes 
extracted environmental values rather than a full environmental raster 
to `ENMevaluate()`, its AICc calculation uses the supplied background predictions 
as an approximation to the environmental domain. Both points matter when 
interpreting or comparing these statistics.

Fold-specific statistics can also be inspected; the `fold` column identifies 
the validation partition:

```{r enmeval-fold-results}
cv_folds <- ENMeval::eval.results.partitions(enmeval_result)

knitr::kable(
  head(cv_folds[, c(
    "tune.args", "fold", "auc.val",
    "tss.val", "thr.val", "tss.train"
  )], 12),
  digits = 3
)
```

Cross-validation helps choose model settings using the training dataset. The 
final model can then be fitted using the selected predictors and model 
settings and evaluated once with the withheld independent test set. In a fully 
nested evaluation of the *complete* modelling procedure, predictor screening 
and other data-dependent preprocessing would also be repeated within each 
cross-validation training fold rather than performed once on all training records.



# Final model selection and independent testing

After evaluating alternative model settings using spatial cross-validation,
the preferred model can be selected from the `ENMevaluation` object.
ENMeval stores models fitted using the complete training dataset for each
combination of feature classes and regularisation multipliers. Consequently,
there is no need to fit the selected model again manually.

The independent testing dataset remains withheld from predictor screening
decisions, model tuning, and fitting.

## Selecting the preferred model

For this introductory example, we select the model with the lowest
corrected Akaike Information Criterion (AICc). Other selection strategies
may also consider cross-validation performance or a combination of
criteria.

```{r select-final-model}
cv_results <- ENMeval::eval.results(enmeval_result)

valid_models <- which(is.finite(cv_results$AICc))

if (!length(valid_models)) {
  stop("No candidate model has a finite AICc.")
}

best_idx <- valid_models[
  which.min(cv_results$AICc[valid_models])
]

best_settings <- cv_results[best_idx, , drop = FALSE]

best_settings[, c(
  "fc", "rm", "tune.args",
  "AICc", "delta.AICc",
  "auc.val.avg", "tss.val.avg"
)]
```

## Extracting the selected model

The `tune.args` column identifies each candidate model within the list
returned by `ENMeval::eval.models()`. We use this identifier to extract
the model fitted with the complete training dataset.

```{r extract-final-model}
best_model_id <- as.character(
  best_settings$tune.args[1]
)

fitted_models <- ENMeval::eval.models(enmeval_result)

final_model <- fitted_models[[best_model_id]]

if (is.null(final_model)) {
  stop("Selected model was not found in enmeval_result.")
}

stopifnot(inherits(final_model, "maxnet"))
```

The resulting `final_model` retains the feature classes, regularisation
multiplier, and background convention used during ENMeval fitting.
No independent testing observations have contributed to this model.

## Selecting a classification threshold

To evaluate threshold-based predictive performance, we first determine
the classification threshold using training predictions only.

Here, `max_tss()` identifies the threshold maximising TSS between
training presences and background records. This threshold will
subsequently be applied unchanged to the independent testing data.

```{r final-training-threshold}
selected_vars <- variance_screen$keep

train_x <- training_set@data[
  , selected_vars, drop = FALSE
]

train_y <- training_set@pa

train_predictions <- predict(
  final_model,
  newdata = train_x,
  type = "cloglog"
)

train_tss <- max_tss(
  p_pos = train_predictions[train_y == 1],
  p_neg = train_predictions[train_y == 0]
)

threshold <- unname(train_tss["threshold"])

train_tss
```



Although this threshold is optimised on the training data, it is selected
without consulting the independent testing observations. Consequently,
its application to the independent dataset provides an assessment of
performance at a previously determined threshold.

## Independent testing

The selected model is now applied to the independently withheld presence
and background records. Only predictors used during model fitting are
included in the prediction dataset.

```{r independent-testing}
test_x <- testing_set@data[
  , selected_vars, drop = FALSE
]

test_y <- testing_set@pa

# Apply ENMeval's clamping convention if enabled
if (isTRUE(enmeval_result@doClamp)) {
  test_x <- ENMeval::clamp.vars(
    orig.vals = test_x,
    ref.vals = train_x,
    left = enmeval_result@clamp.directions$left,
    right = enmeval_result@clamp.directions$right
  )
}

test_predictions <- predict(
  final_model,
  newdata = test_x,
  type = "cloglog"
)

test_pos <- test_predictions[test_y == 1]
test_bg <- test_predictions[test_y == 0]

test_sensitivity <- mean(test_pos >= threshold)
test_specificity <- mean(test_bg < threshold)

independent_tss <-
  test_sensitivity + test_specificity - 1

independent_results <- data.frame(
  model = best_model_id,
  n_presences = length(test_pos),
  n_background = length(test_bg),
  threshold = threshold,
  sensitivity = test_sensitivity,
  background_specificity = test_specificity,
  TSS = independent_tss
)

knitr::kable(
  independent_results,
  digits = 3,
  caption = "Independent testing results for the selected Maxnet model."
)
```

Sensitivity represents the proportion of independently withheld
presences classified as suitable, whereas background-based specificity
represents the proportion of withheld background records classified as
unsuitable.

Because background locations are not confirmed absences, TSS should be
interpreted as a measure of discrimination between presences and
background rather than conventional presence-absence classification
accuracy.

The classification threshold was selected using the training dataset
and was not re-optimised on the independent testing data. Furthermore,
neither the model settings nor the predictor set were modified after
examining the independent testing results.

This provides an independent assessment of the completed modelling
procedure at a preselected classification threshold.
